title: Witnesses describe out-of-control seizures ; INQUEST: A CORONER'S JURY HEARS LOGAN SCHAAFSMA HAD TO BE SEDATED BEFORE OFFICERS COULD CONTROL HIM ENOUGH TO GET HIM TO HOSPITAL BUT HE DIED UPON ARRIVAL
article: On the last day of his life, Logan Schaafsma was out of control.

Two hours after having the worst grand mal seizures he ever had, the 20-year old man who required constant care at the Agano Resources Group Home on Clarke Rd. was dead of cardiorespiratory arrest at London's Victoria Hospital.
A jury at a coroner's inquest examining Schaafsma's death heard Thursday that his heart stopped because of post ictal (after seizure) excited delirium while coming out of a series of seizures.

The inquest at the Middlesex County building has heard how group home workers, paramedics and police tried to calm the aggressive Schaafsma, who was thrashing and lashing out at people on Aug. 3, 2010.
He was in police custody when he died.
The inquest, overseen by Dr. John Ewen, is looking into the events leading up to Schaafsma's death.
Pathologist Edward Tweedie presented his conclusions to the jury, pointing out one of the causes of excited delirium comes from seizures.
Schaafsma, required two workers at the group home 'round the clock.
On the day of his death, his workers called for paramedics after Schaafsma started to have a seizure.
Paramedic Deborah Hunter testified she and her partner knocked on the door of the group home and had to step back when Schaafsma came charging outside.
His arms were flailing and he was making noises. "He took swings at the paramedics and they backed off.
Two female London police officers arrived and tried to communicate with him.
While they tried to restrain Schaafsma, Hunter said, she got a binder of information from the two female workers and had a few seconds to skim through it.
The jury heard from Terrence Johnson, 57, a self-employed Londoner who for 27 years was a manager in federal prisons across the country.
He was driving by and saw the struggle between Schaafsma and the police.
He stopped his SUV and got out to help. "Everyone was yelling 'calm down, calm down, calm down,' " he said.
The officers were trying to handcuff Schaafsma. "It was escalating," Johnson said. "It was a violent struggle."
Johnson helped the officers by grabbing Schaafsma's left arm and tried to gently get him to the ground.
"The strength of this individual was unbelievable," he said. Schaafsma was kicking and banging his head on the ground. The workers were yelling "he doesn't feel pain."
Schaafsma was cuffed and zip ties were put around his legs.
More officers arrived and Hunter testified she tried to put an oxygen mask on him and check vital signs.
Eventually he was put on a stretcher and another paramedic, Robert Gee, arrived to give him a sedative.
Gee testified he received the proper go-ahead from a doctor to give the medication.
He was told by the workers the sedative had worked on Schaafsma before.
It took eight anxious minutes after he was given drugs through his nose that Schaafsma finally started to calm down.
Gee said they were ready to take Schaafsma to the hospital when he stopped breathing.
Within minutes, they brought him back and got him into the ambulance.
Schaafsma was handcuffed to the rails of the stretcher.
On the way to Victoria Hospital, Gee said, Schaafsma started to seize again.
More medication was given but "it was futile," Gee said.
"You were hoping the drug would take him out of seizure and it didn't," he said.
Schaafsma died at the hospital. None of the witnesses reported seeing the police being aggressive or inappropriate with Schaafsma.
The inquest continues Friday. He lived at a London group home and required constant care.
His death is being investigated because he was in police custody when he died in hospital.
